conserved_row.complete_before_row: 2.3 The quotient $\Lambda_2/(t_1-1)$ is $\mathbb Z[t_2^{\pm1}]$, a domain by [F5], so $t_1-1$ is prime. It does not divide $t_2-1$, whose image under $t_1\mapsto1$ is the nonzero element $t_2-1$. If $(a,b)$ lies in the kernel, $(t_1-1)a=-(t_2-1)b$, so primality forces $t_1-1$ to divide $b$. Write $b=(t_1-1)c$; cancellation in the domain gives $a=-(t_2-1)c$. Thus the kernel is generated by $(-(t_2-1),t_1-1)$; it is free because its second coordinate can vanish only when $c=0$. Hence $A_U\cong\Lambda_2$. [F4, F5, step 2.2, algebra]

conserved_row.complete_before_row: 1.2 The long exact sequence of the actual short exact sequence $CF^-\to CF^\infty\to CF^+$ identifies the image in plus homology, with its grading, as $R\rho/U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have exponents $j<a$, so their least degree is $\deg\rho-2(a-1)$, attained at $U^{a-1}\rho$. Sending the standard tower element $U^k$ to $U^{k+a-1}\rho$ identifies the image with $R/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ shifted by this least degree. Multiplying any individual element sufficiently many times by $U$ kills it, while decreasing exponents supplies a preimage under any power of $U$. This proves all the tower assertions. [step 1.1]

conserved_row.complete_before_row: 1.2 The surgery retains the old oriented surface outside the two attaching disks, so its positive normal there is unchanged and the old matrix block remains $V$. Use product coordinates $(t,w)$ on the cylinder, with $w\in D^2$, and take $c=\{t_0\}\times\partial D^2$. Let $b$ follow one longitudinal side of the tube and return through $F_0$; it crosses each cross-section disk once. The disks $\{t_0\}\times D^2$ and their sufficiently close parallel disks miss every old basis curve and its push-off, so [F4] gives zero for the two Seifert pairings between $c$ and every old basis curve. Along the lateral annulus, the positive normal points either out of or into the solid cylinder. If it points out, the radius-one cross-section disk misses $b^+$, giving $V(b,c)=0$, while the disk of slightly larger radius bounds $c^+$ and meets $b$ once; it gives $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=+1$ after orienting $c$, hence $V(c,b)=+1$ by the symmetry in [F4]. If it points in, the radius-one disk meets $b^+$ once, giving $V(b,c)=+1$ after orienting $c$, while the disk of slightly smaller radius bounds $c^+$ and misses $b$, giving $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=0$ and therefore $V(c,b)=0$. These intersection statements follow from the explicit single transverse point in the product coordinates and [F4]. In either case the concentric parallel meridians have $V(c,c)=0$. The remaining entries involving $b$ are integers $x$, $y$, and $z=\operatorname{lk}(b^+,b)$. Thus in the ordered basis $(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b,c)$ the matrix has exactly one of the two displayed forms. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎
